summary: Extends TURN, a relay protocol for NAT traversal, so a client can request TCP allocations. It defines new requests and indications for the TURN server to open and accept TCP connections with the client's peers.

plainLanguage.summary: TURN is a helper that passes messages when firewalls block direct contact. This lets that helper also relay full TCP connections, not just loose packets.

questions: turn relay tcp connections nat traversal
how does turn relay tcp connections
what is a turn connectionbind request
subtitle: Lets a TURN client get a TCP relay address and open TCP connections through the server to its peers.

tldr.problem: TURN could only allocate UDP ports on a server, but some sessions need TCP with a peer while NATs block a direct TCP connection.
tldr.mechanism: The client asks for a TCP allocation over a control connection, then uses Connect, ConnectionAttempt and ConnectionBind to pair each client data connection with a peer data connection, which the server relays as-is.
tldr.outcome: A client can make and accept relayed TCP connections, but the extension deliberately restricts how the relayed address is used so it cannot host a general-purpose server.

today: RFC 6062 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5766.

sections.title: Why TURN Needs TCP Allocations
sections.content:
TURN (RFC 5766) lets a client ask a server to allocate a port on one of its interfaces and relay traffic between that port and the client. With STUN and ICE it forms a NAT traversal solution for UDP-based media sessions.

TURN itself gives no way to allocate a TCP-based port. That is needed when a TCP session is wanted with a peer and NATs prevent a direct TCP connection. The RFC gives application sharing between desktop softphones and sending pictures during a voice session as examples.

A TCP allocation is a TURN allocation that uses TCP instead of UDP. It is identified by its relayed transport address, an IP address plus a TCP port.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper used to pass only loose notes. Sometimes two people need a steady conversation instead, so the helper needs a way to hold that line open.

sections.title: Control and Data Connections
sections.content:
The client has two kinds of connections to its TURN server. One control connection exists per allocated relayed transport address. It carries only TURN messages and is used to get allocations and open new connections. For each peer connection there is also a data connection: a client data connection between client and server, and a peer data connection between server and peer.

After an initial TURN message binds the two data connections together, only application data can be sent on them, with no TURN messaging. The server forwards data without any encapsulation or framing. Closing one data connection closes the other, so the client always knows the state of the connection.

Flow control is end to end: if the relay cannot write to the destination, it stops reading from the source.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one line just for talking to the helper about arrangements. Then for each friend, there is a separate private line where only the real conversation goes through.

sections.title: Client Procedures
sections.content:
To create a TCP allocation, the client opens a TCP or TLS connection to the server, since TCP allocations cannot be obtained over UDP. It sends an Allocate request whose REQUESTED-TRANSPORT attribute is 6, meaning TCP. The request MUST NOT include DONT-FRAGMENT, RESERVATION-TOKEN or EVEN-PORT, but may include LIFETIME. Refresh requests MUST be sent on the control connection.

To reach a peer, the client sends a Connect request on the control connection with an XOR-PEER-ADDRESS. The success response contains a CONNECTION-ID. The client then opens a new TCP connection to the same server address, from a different local transport address, authenticates the same way, and sends a ConnectionBind request echoing the identifier.

If Connect fails with error 447, the client MAY retry the same peer address but MUST wait at least 10 seconds. Connect requests with the same peer address MUST NOT be sent simultaneously. For incoming connections, the client receives a ConnectionAttempt indication and binds in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the helper whom you want to reach on the talking line. The helper gives you a ticket number, and you open a new private line and show the ticket so the helper can connect it to your friend.

sections.title: Server Behavior
sections.content:
For a TCP Allocate request the server follows RFC 5766 with exceptions. It rejects a transport other than UDP or TCP with 442. It rejects a request not sent over TCP or TLS, or one containing DONT-FRAGMENT, EVEN-PORT or RESERVATION-TOKEN, with 400. It allocates a TCP relayed address and starts accepting connections on it.

On a Connect request the server returns 437 if no allocation exists, 446 if a connection to the same peer is already being made or exists, 400 for a missing or invalid peer address, and 403 if local policy forbids it. Otherwise it opens a TCP connection from the relayed address, and a failure or timeout gives 447. The timeout MUST be at least 30 seconds. On success it buffers data from the client and returns a unique CONNECTION-ID.

When a peer connects to the relayed address, the server accepts it, but closes it immediately if no permission is installed for that peer. Otherwise it sends a ConnectionAttempt indication with the peer address and connection identifier. In both cases, a peer data connection is closed if no ConnectionBind arrives within 30 seconds.

A ConnectionBind request must refer to an existing pending connection, or the server returns 400. After it, data is relayed as-is both ways, including data buffered earlier. If the allocation expires, data connections are closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper checks every request carefully and says no with a number when something is wrong. If nobody claims a waiting call within 30 seconds, the helper hangs up.

sections.title: New STUN Codes
sections.content: The RFC adds three STUN methods: 0x000a Connect, 0x000b ConnectionBind and 0x000c ConnectionAttempt. It adds one attribute, CONNECTION-ID (0x002a), a 32-bit unsigned integer that uniquely identifies a peer data connection. It also adds two error codes: 446 Connection Already Exists and 447 Connection Timeout or Failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The new commands and error messages each get an official number so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Between the TCP connection to the peer and the arrival of ConnectionBind, the server buffers all data from the peer. The server may drop the connection if the buffer is about to exceed a limit defined by local policy, which should make sure memory is not exhausted. The RFC points to RFC 4732. All security considerations of STUN (RFC 5389) and TURN (RFC 5766) also apply.

The abstract adds that TURN and this extension purposefully restrict how the relayed address can be used, so users cannot run general-purpose servers from ports obtained from the TURN server.
sections.plainLanguage: While the helper waits for you to pick up, it holds incoming messages in a box. The box has a size limit so a flood of messages cannot fill the whole room.
